video_title: President Alexander Stubb: Who Decides the New World Order? | Podcast | In Good Company
gist: Finnish President Alexander Stubb argues the post-1989 world order is dissolving into a contest between a reformed multilateral UN system and multipolar transactional chaos, with the Global South (not the East) gaining decisive weight, AI/compute/energy access becoming a new axis of power that already rivals nation-states, and Europe forced into a more geopolitical, defense-heavy posture by Russia and an unpredictable Trump administration.

themes.theme: Global South Ascendance & World Order Reset

insights.claim: The post-Cold War world order is undergoing its fourth major reset (after 1918, 1945, 1989), and the outcome will be decided by the Global South's choice between a reformed multilateral/UN-based order and a multipolar, transactional, conflict-prone system.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Investors should track UN Security Council reform and Global South coalition-building (not just US-China rivalry) as the key variable for how stable or fragmented the geopolitical/trade environment becomes over the next decade.
insights.quote: The most important message is that the world order is changing much like it changed in 1918, 1945 and 1989.

insights.claim: Western dominance is ending not because the East (China) is taking over, but because the Global South (India, Gulf states, Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt, Brazil, Argentina) now has the population, economic, and technological scale to set terms itself.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Reframes the standard 'US vs China' investment narrative; capital flows, demand growth and diplomatic leverage should increasingly be modeled around a fragmented multipolar Global South rather than a simple bipolar rivalry.

insights.claim: China has consistently outplayed Europe in the Global South by funding hard infrastructure (airports, highways, hotels), while European leaders show up mainly to lecture on governance, entrenching a durable Chinese soft-power and commercial advantage across Africa and other developing regions.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Chinese-linked infrastructure, construction and commodities plays in Africa/Global South carry an entrenched incumbency advantage over European competitors unless European policy shifts from criticism to co-investment.
insights.quote: A western leader came to an African country, landed at an airport which was built by the Chinese, drove down a highway which was built by the Chinese... saying that you should not be cooperating with the Chinese.

insights.claim: Stubb and Mark Carney argue a fourth power bloc is emerging built on compute, data and AI, meaning technology leadership itself is becoming a geopolitical power center alongside (not just within) the US, China and the Global South, and access to it should be structured as win-win rather than zero-sum.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Frames AI infrastructure (compute capacity, data, chips, energy) as a distinct strategic asset class investors and policymakers should track the way they track military or trade power, not merely as a tech-sector story.

themes.theme: AI Power, Big Tech vs. States, and the Governance Gap

insights.claim: Stubb explicitly questions whether Anthropic or Facebook (Meta) is now more powerful than sovereign states like Norway or Finland, and says political science has no clear answer to the question.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Signals that even sitting heads of state now treat frontier AI labs and platform companies as peer-level power centers to nation-states, which should raise the bar for how investors price regulatory/geopolitical risk around Big Tech and AI labs.
insights.quote: So you can ask the question, you know, is Anthropic or is Facebook more powerful than Norway and Finland? And I think it's a legitimate question and political science can't necessarily give you the answer.

insights.claim: Dominance in AI requires two specific inputs: compute/data capacity and energy (electricity), and global power balance between the US, China, Europe and the Global South will hinge on differential access to these two resources.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Reinforces the thesis that power grid capacity, chip supply and data-center energy access are now strategic bottlenecks worth tracking as directly as semiconductor export controls.
insights.quote: If you want to dominate you need two things: you need compute... and secondly you need energy or more specifically electricity.

insights.claim: Democracies are structurally losing the adaptation race to social media and AI because democratic institutions were designed in the 1700s to be deliberately slow and consensus-based, unlike the always-on reaction speed modern technology demands.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Supports a base case of continued regulatory lag and policy whiplash around AI/platforms in democracies, favoring jurisdictions or firms that can move faster than legislatures (both a risk and an opportunity for AI-first companies).
insights.quote: Democracies have not been able to cope with social media and with modern technology yet, and they're losing the struggle.

insights.claim: AI could either equalize opportunity globally or amplify injustice depending on near-term policy choices, and the mix of biotechnology with AI (DNA manipulation, genome sequencing) risks creating a Harari-style 'useless class' by removing the economic leverage labor historically held even under capitalism.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: A structural labor-displacement risk that could reshape political stability and consumption patterns over the next decade; worth watching as a driver of populist/polarization risk premiums.

insights.claim: Because formal regulation lags fast-moving technology by one to three years, Stubb argues governance should rely on dedicated frontier-AI control bodies (citing Demis Hassabis's AI-safety work) starting in the US, then Europe and China, before eventually rolling up into a UN-level governance structure.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Suggests the realistic near-term AI governance path is technical/lab-led safety bodies rather than binding international law, which matters for how investors assess frontier-AI regulatory tail risk (e.g., catastrophic cyberattack scenarios) versus compliance-cost risk.
insights.quote: We need some kind of control bodies that can deal with this and make sure that frontier AI doesn't give us an apocalyptic result in for instance cyber attacks.

themes.theme: European Defense Rearmament & NATO's Burden Shift

insights.claim: NATO members are raising the defense-spending target from 2% to 5% of GDP, with defense industries described as 'booming' across both Europe and the United States.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Directly supports a multi-year European/US defense-industrial capex and order-book tailwind; a concrete spending-target data point to size the sector opportunity.
insights.quote: I wouldn't say an alliance is in a crisis when it's increasing its defense expenditure from 2% to 5%, when defense industries are booming all around Europe and the United States.

insights.claim: Finland maintained high defense spending and preparedness after the Cold War (despite not joining NATO until 2023) due to memory of the 1939-1944 wars with the Soviet Union, buying 64 F-18 fighter jets, keeping male conscription, and buying secondary-market artillery.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: A concrete case study of sustained defense-industrial demand driven by historical threat memory rather than current-year headlines — a template for assessing which countries will sustain elevated defense capex even after any Ukraine ceasefire.

insights.claim: Because Finland's defense posture was already highly NATO-compatible, its 2023 NATO accession negotiations were the fastest in the alliance's history after applying following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Illustrates how pre-existing interoperability (equipment standards, doctrine) compresses political/accession timelines — relevant for gauging how fast other partner states (e.g., further NATO enlargement candidates) could formalize alliances.

insights.claim: NATO is shifting from a US-anchored posture toward one where European members take more responsibility for conventional forces (land, air, navy, cyber, space) as the US signals it will not provide certain capabilities even in peacetime or crisis, requiring Europe to build domestic replacements.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Points to a structural, multi-year demand shift toward European-built military hardware and capability gap-fillers (land forces, navy, cyber, space) as US-provided capabilities are withdrawn — a specific sourcing/localization theme for European defense contractors.

insights.claim: The US is buying 11 icebreakers under a bilateral defense/industrial arrangement with Finland, with 4 built in Finland and 7 built in the United States.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: A concrete, named cross-border defense-industrial order (Arctic/icebreaker capacity) that signals US reliance on Finnish shipbuilding expertise — a specific data point for Arctic infrastructure and shipyard order-book tracking.

insights.claim: Stubb predicts Ukraine achieves a 'defense victory' (preserved sovereignty and independence, not necessarily territorial reconquest), noting Ukraine is currently stronger militarily, politically and financially than at any prior point in the war, while Russia's battlefield and economic losses are outpacing Ukraine's.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: A senior European head-of-state's base case for war outcome and relative attrition, useful context for sizing Ukraine reconstruction, European sanctions-policy durability, and Russia-exposed asset risk.
insights.quote: I see a defense victory in the cards for Ukraine.

insights.claim: Over half of the Russian population now wants the war to end, and Stubb argues the war will conclude not from economic collapse or bank runs, nor from battlefield losses alone, but from domestic political pressure on the Russian regime.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Suggests investors should watch Russian domestic sentiment/polling and internal political signals as the leading indicator for war termination, more than sanctions-driven economic indicators or front-line maps.
insights.quote: It's not going to end because of economic problems for Russia or bank runs... but it will end if the current regime feels a pressure from the population.

insights.claim: Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries and logistics centers are causing domestic fuel rationing inside Russia, which is a direct mechanism building the internal political pressure that could push Russia toward ending the war.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable transmission channel (refinery strikes to at the pump rationing to political pressure) to monitor via Russian fuel-price/rationing reports as a war-progress proxy, alongside energy-market spillover from reduced Russian refining capacity.
insights.quote: Ukraine is successfully hitting oil refineries, which then hits the gas pump of the Ukrainians where they have rationing and limits.

insights.claim: The line between war and peace is 'blurred' by hybrid warfare — undersea cable cutting, drone incursions over airports, GPS jamming, cyberattacks and sabotage attributed to Russia and other state/non-state actors — which Stubb says does not yet meet the threshold for NATO Article 5 activation.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Frames current European infrastructure disruption (cables, GPS, drones) as a sustained sub-threshold campaign rather than isolated incidents, relevant for insuring/assessing critical infrastructure, subsea cable and aviation risk in the Baltic/Nordic region.

themes.theme: Europe's Geopolitical Awakening & the Trump Effect

insights.claim: Stubb says he is more bullish on European unity now than at any point since he entered European affairs in the early 1990s, citing Brexit (which unified the remaining 27), COVID vaccine procurement, the Ukraine war response, and current US tariff pressure as the unifying catalysts — but warns that unity could erode once the Ukraine war ends and the US administration changes.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: A senior insider's explicit, time-bound bull case for EU cohesion with a stated expiry condition (end of war + US administration change) — a concrete catalyst/risk pair for European integration and EU-asset risk premia to monitor.
insights.quote: I've never seen Europe more united than it is right now... pressure from the east and pressure from the west has united Europe quite strongly.

insights.claim: The EU has accelerated free trade agreements with India, Mercosur, Japan and South Korea, partly as a diversification response to unreliable/tariff-heavy US trade policy.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Signals accelerating EU trade diversification away from US dependency — relevant for sizing new EU trade-linked export/investment flows into India, Mercosur (Brazil/Argentina), Japan and South Korea.

insights.claim: Canada under Mark Carney is actively pursuing closer alignment with the EU (rather than the US) in response to US tariff pressure, with Stubb half-jokingly preferring Canada as a 28th EU member over being a '51st US state.'
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: A concrete signal of Canada-EU trade/political realignment underway, worth tracking for Canadian export diversification and EU-Canada deal flow as a hedge against US tariff exposure.
insights.quote: I'd much rather see Canada as the 28th member state of the EU rather than the 51st state of the United States.

insights.claim: Stubb frames his foreign-policy doctrine as 'values-based realism': holding firm to democratic/rule-of-law values while accepting that global problems (climate, AI, energy) cannot be solved unilaterally and require compromise with actors who don't share those values, resulting in a proliferation of messy, interest-based ad hoc coalitions rather than a clean multilateral order.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Sets expectations for continued policy fragmentation and shifting-coalition diplomacy (rather than stable blocs) as the near-term operating environment for cross-border deals and multilateral negotiations.
insights.quote: It's going to be extremely messy and we're starting to see that already.

insights.claim: Stubb calls Trump 'one of the most consequential presidents in American history' who is forcing change domestically and globally, and argues Europeans' real blind spot is refusing to acknowledge how effective Trump is, rather than any deeper misunderstanding of his agenda.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Argues for pragmatic engagement over resistance as the effective European strategy toward the Trump administration — relevant for gauging how quickly European governments will cut bilateral deals (defense, trade, Ukraine) versus posture in opposition.
insights.quote: You have to understand that President Trump is one of the most consequential presidents in American history... it's probably that they don't understand or want to admit that President Trump is very effective in what he does.

themes.theme: Polarization and Social Cohesion as Political Risk

insights.claim: Stubb names polarization and inequality as the biggest threat to societal stability, singling out the United States as 'probably the most polarized liberal democracy in the world,' and links it to the failure of globalization to deliver broadly on its promise of shared prosperity.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: Ties populist/political risk directly to perceived distributional failure of free trade and institutions — a framework for pricing political risk premia in markets where inequality perception is rising, especially the US.

insights.claim: Finland has been ranked the happiest country in the world for nine consecutive years, which Stubb attributes to a strong welfare-state safety net, high education levels, and close connection to nature rather than any single economic metric.
insights.speaker: Alexander Stubb
insights.so_what: A social-stability data point supporting a low political-risk premium for Nordic sovereign and corporate exposure relative to more polarized peer democracies.
